content.title: About
content.content: Spinach is a leafy vegetable belonging to the Amaranthaceae family. It is cultivated in temperate regions and is commonly used fresh in salads, sandwiches, as well as in cooked dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach is high in iron, but its absorption improves when paired with vitamin C.
Spinach was known in ancient Rome and Greece.
Its oxalate content can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.
There are several varieties: flat‑leaf, curly, and savoy (Latin).
Spinach is often used as a natural green food coloring.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision and immunity.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is needed for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie fiber source
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate levels may increase the risk of kidney stones in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Raw leaves can carry pesticide residues; wash thoroughly or choose organic.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spinach can be added to sandwiches, salads, smoothies, or lightly sautéed or stewed. For sandwiches, use fresh young leaves, rinsed and patted dry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store spinach in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container lined with a damp paper towel. Use within 3–5 days. Frozen spinach should be kept in an airtight bag for up to 6 months.
